l: Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Roxie Fairfield Daymon and her husband Daymon leave Louisville for Chicago, where Daymon becomes wealthy through land dealings, but Roxie later dies of cholera without learning Susan Lasco's fate. After the burning of the Brandywine on the Mississippi River, John A. Lasco dies leaving a bequest to Susan Lasco and her descendants. Brindle Bill and S. S. Simon use evidence linking Rose Simon Fairfield to Susan Lasco and Tom Fairfield to obtain the Lasco inheritance, while concealing Rose's sisters. Rose later dies of yellow fever in Louisiana, intestate and childless.

l: Roxie Fairfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Roxie Fairfield runs away with her lover, marries him according to common law, and becomes Daymon's wife. She helps build their life in Chicago and becomes wealthy, but dies of cholera, leaving an only daughter and remaining unaware of Susan Lasco's fate.

l: John A. Lasco, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: John A. Lasco searches for his sister Susan Lasco in America for three years. After surviving the burning of the Brandywine only briefly, he dictates a statement leaving twenty thousand dollars to Susan Lasco and her descendants and one hundred ten dollars to the woman caring for him.

l: Susan Lasco, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Susan Lasco is John A. Lasco's sister and the daughter of the man who emigrated with her from the old country. She married Tom Fairfield and became the mother of Rose Simon Fairfield and other daughters.

l: Brindle Bill, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Brindle Bill recognizes Susan Lasco's name in John A. Lasco's dying statement and connects it to Rose Simon's mother. He conspires with S. S. Simon and Sundown Hill to obtain the Lasco inheritance by falsely claiming that Rose's sisters are dead, and later pressures Simon for additional money.

l: S. S. Simon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: S. S. Simon helps Brindle Bill establish Rose's claim to the Lasco inheritance and persuades Rose to let him manage the matter. He participates in the false testimony, receives the money, and uses Rose's share to advance himself as a planter and build a new house.

l: Rose Fairfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Rose Simon Fairfield is identified as the daughter of Susan Lasco and Tom Fairfield through a breast-pin and a marriage certificate. She receives the Lasco inheritance after false testimony that she is the only surviving child, but dies of yellow fever on the way home from New Orleans, intestate and childless.

l: Tom Fairfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Tom Fairfield was married to Susan Lasco and was the father of Rose Simon Fairfield and her sisters. His marriage to Susan is documented by a certificate kept among Rose's family keepsakes.

l: Chicago, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Daymon and Roxie move to Chicago, Illinois, where Daymon works as a day laborer before accepting fifteen acres of land for a debt owed to him. Chicago's rapid growth allows him to sell land at increasing prices and become wealthy.

l: Mississippi River, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: The Brandywine burns on the Mississippi River after being driven onto a deep sand bar, causing many passengers to drown or be killed by the fire.

l: Shirt-Tail Bend, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Shirt-Tail Bend is where S. S. Simon lives and where Brindle Bill returns to pursue the Lasco inheritance scheme. Simon later becomes a prominent planter in the neighborhood.

l: Port William, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Port William, at the mouth of the Kentucky River, is identified as the place where Rose Simon and her sisters were separated.

l: Brandywine, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: The Brandywine burns late at night while heavily loaded with passengers and freight. John A. Lasco reaches shore badly injured and dies after giving his account of the Lasco family estate and inheritance.

l: family estate (the Lasco family estate), Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: The Lasco family estate had been held in abeyance because family papers were lost. After the papers are recovered, John A. Lasco sells the property and deposits twenty thousand dollars in a western bank for Susan Lasco and her descendants.

l: Lasco family papers, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: The Lasco family papers are recovered after a condemned man, Alonzo Phelps, confesses where he concealed them. John A. Lasco carries papers identifying the bank holding the inheritance, and the papers are entrusted to the woman caring for him to dry and deliver to a respectable lawyer in Memphis.

l: John A. Lasco's bequest, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: John A. Lasco's bequest gives twenty thousand dollars deposited in a western bank to Susan Lasco and her descendants. He also leaves the one hundred ten dollars in his pocket to the woman of the cabin who cared for him.

l: Susan Lasco's breast-pin, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Susan Lasco's breast-pin bears the inscription, "Presented to Susan Lasco by her brother, John A. Lasco, 1751." Rose Simon produces it as evidence of her connection to John A. Lasco.

l: Tom Fairfield and Susan Lasco marriage certificate, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: The marriage certificate of Tom Fairfield and Susan Lasco had been kept for years in Rose Simon's box of family keepsakes. Rose produces it along with the breast-pin when claiming the Lasco inheritance.

l: burning of the Brandywine, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: During the burning of the Brandywine, the pilot directs the vessel toward the wrong shore, where it grounds on a deep sand bar and burns to the water's edge. Many passengers drown, while others escape on pieces of the wreck.

l: Lasco inheritance fraud, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: The Lasco inheritance fraud is carried out by Brindle Bill, S. S. Simon, and Sundown Hill. They falsely testify that Rose Simon Fairfield is the only surviving child of Tom Fairfield and Susan Lasco, obtain the twenty thousand dollars, and use the threat of locating her sisters to extract further payments from Simon.

l: yellow fever, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FOURTH--ROXIE DAYMON AND ROSE SIMON.
s: Rose Simon Fairfield is attacked by yellow fever while traveling in New Orleans to select furniture for her new house. She dies on the way home and is buried in Louisiana.

l: Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Suza Fairfield is captured by Tom Ditamus at the request of the Demitt relations but escapes during the night and returns to Aunt Katy Demitt in Port William. Aunt Katy reveals her savings and a will leaving all her possessions to Suza. More than a decade later, Don Carlo attends a camp meeting, learns that Suza is the young woman who rescued him from the Red Stone wreck, and begins courting her. The neighborhood soon says that Suza and Don Carlo are engaged.

l: Suza Fairfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Suza Fairfield, an eleven-year-old orphan raised by Aunt Katy Demitt, is abducted by Tom Ditamus but escapes by deceiving him and traveling through the woods back to Port William. She later becomes the belle of Port William and meets Don Carlo at a camp meeting.

l: Aunt Katy Demitt, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Aunt Katy Demitt lives in Port William with Suza Fairfield, earns money by knitting stockings, and keeps her affairs private. After Suza returns, Aunt Katy reveals that the Demitt relations wanted Suza removed and confirms that she has left her possessions to Suza.

l: Don Carlo, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Don Carlo survives the Red Stone explosion and later purchases a small farm in Kentucky. At a camp meeting he recognizes Suza Fairfield as the woman who rescued him and begins riding with her toward Port William.

l: Tom Ditamus, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Tom Ditamus agrees to take Suza Fairfield to the backwoods of the Cumberland Mountains for ten dollars. He captures her, but she tricks him and escapes while he and his family sleep; Tom then continues traveling after discovering her absence.

l: Demitt relations, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: The Demitt relations speculate about Aunt Katy's money and believe that Suza Fairfield may inherit it. They arrange for Tom Ditamus to take Suza away so that Aunt Katy will not hear from her and the money may eventually pass to them.

l: Port William, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Port William is the village where Aunt Katy and Suza Fairfield live. Suza returns there after her escape, and it is later the home of the belle Suza and the place toward which she and Don Carlo ride after the camp meeting.

l: Ohio River, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: The Ohio River is visible from the broad bottom land near Port William. Suza Fairfield recognizes the river landscape and the chimneys of Port William as she completes her return home.

l: Kentucky River, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Suza Fairfield follows the Kentucky River during her escape because she knows it will lead her to Port William. When the road diverges, she travels through woods and underbrush along the river until she can rejoin the road.

l: Shirt-Tail Bend, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Don Carlo had been associated with Shirt-Tail Bend and had sold out there before returning toward his childhood home. He is later identified as the hero of Shirt-Tail Bend.

l: the Red Stone, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: The Red Stone is connected with the wreck in which Don Carlo was left senseless after an explosion. Suza Fairfield is later identified as the young woman who pulled Don Carlo from the river after the accident.

l: the half-way castle, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: The half-way castle is an early brick house on the southern bank of the Ohio River, about halfway between Louisville and Cincinnati. Don Carlo is left there in a severely stunned but nonfatal condition after the Red Stone accident.

l: Aunt Katy's money, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Aunt Katy's money is the subject of speculation among the Demitt relations. Aunt Katy shows Suza Fairfield five hundred dollars in gold and silver that she has saved through her own work and economy.

l: Aunt Katy's will, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Aunt Katy's will is witnessed by old Ballard and old Father Tearful. It bequeaths all of Aunt Katy's earthly possessions to Suza Fairfield.

l: Suza Fairfield's capture, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Tom Ditamus captures Suza Fairfield in a foggy morning near his camp, threatening her with a gag and placing her in his covered wagon. He takes her south with his wife and children toward the backwoods of the Cumberland Mountains.

l: Suza Fairfield's escape, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Suza Fairfield escapes at night after persuading Tom Ditamus that she hates Aunt Katy and would go anywhere to leave her. She follows the Kentucky River, crosses White's Creek at a ford, rejoins the road, and reaches Aunt Katy's house in Port William by dawn.

l: Red Stone explosion, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: The Red Stone explosion leaves Don Carlo severely stunned but not fatally injured. The accident occurs as he is returning toward the home of his childhood.

l: Don Carlo's rescue, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: A brave young woman rushes into the water and drags Don Carlo's lifeless body to shore after the Red Stone wreck. At the camp meeting, Don learns that the rescuer is Suza Fairfield.

l: camp meeting, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: A camp meeting is held near Port William, with preaching, prayer meetings, love feasts, and visitors camping in the woods. Don Carlo attends it hoping to meet the young woman who saved him and there sees Suza Fairfield.

l: Don Carlo and Suza Fairfield's courtship, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE FIFTH.
s: Don Carlo is immediately attracted to Suza Fairfield at the camp meeting and learns that she is his rescuer. They ride side by side toward Port William, and the neighborhood says that they are engaged to be married.

l: Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The Second Generation introduces Young Simon, heir to S. S. Simon's plantations and slaves, and follows his father's death, his own short life, and the early life of his cousin Cæsar Simon. Cæsar, later calling himself Cole Conway, becomes a gambler and meets Steve Brindle, who reveals that he is Steve Sharp's partner and the son of Brindle Bill. Cæsar tells Brindle about his family, and Brindle identifies him as the heir to S. S. Simon's large estate in Arkansas. The unit also describes the expansion of cotton cultivation and slavery in the Western States, the arrival of the iron horse and magnetic telegraph, and Cæsar's dream of a steam carriage.

l: The Second Generation, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The Second Generation begins after the characters from the preceding part have died or passed from the stage of life. It follows descendants including Young Simon and Cæsar Simon as they confront inheritance, poverty, gambling, and the consequences of family history.

l: Young Simon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Young Simon is the only son of S. S. Simon by a second wife, and his mother is dead. He inherits four plantations of one thousand acres each and more than six hundred slaves, but he has poor health, little family knowledge, and dies young.

l: S. S. Simon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: S. S. Simon owns four large plantations and more than six hundred slaves and works relentlessly to die a rich man. He knows the history of Roxie Daymon or Roxie Fairfield and dies from swamp fever after deliriously crying, "Take Roxie Daymon away."

l: Cæsar Simon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Cæsar Simon is the son of S. S. Simon's brother and is raised by his impoverished sisters, "big-sis" and "little-sis." Imaginative, mischievous, and averse to work, he later leaves Tennessee, becomes a gambler, and learns that he is heir to S. S. Simon's estate.

l: Cole Conway, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Cæsar Simon uses the name Cole Conway when he lives in Paducah, Kentucky, and partners with Steve Sharp in gambling. After losing their money, he tells Steve Brindle his true name and family history.

l: Steve Brindle, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Steve Brindle is the name used by Steve Sharp, whose father was Brindle Bill and whose mother was a sister of Sundown Hill. He tells Cole Conway that he is a child born outside marriage and recognizes Conway as Cæsar Simon, heir to S. S. Simon's estate in Arkansas.

l: Steve Sharp, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Steve Sharp is Cole Conway's gambling partner in Paducah, Kentucky. He later identifies himself as Steve Brindle and exchanges family histories with Conway.

l: Roxie Daymon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Roxie Daymon, also called Roxie Fairfield, is connected to the hidden history of S. S. Simon's family. S. S. Simon believes that she or her descendants may still survive, and her name torments him during his final illness.

l: Roxie Fairfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Roxie Fairfield is the alias of Roxie Daymon. Her history is known to S. S. Simon up to the time she left Louisville, but Cæsar Simon and Steve Brindle do not learn that part of the family history in this unit.

l: Western States, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The Western States undergo rapid settlement and progress during the decade from 1840 to 1850. The iron horse and magnetic telegraph are successfully put into operation across them.

l: West and Southwest, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The history of the West and Southwest during the first half of the nineteenth century is described as full of romance and truth stranger than fiction. The region experiences the rise of a moneyed aristocracy and the rapid expansion of cotton cultivation and slavery.

l: Mississippi River, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The Mississippi River region is associated with the expansion of plantations, cotton cultivation, and slavery. S. S. Simon's plantation work extends along the Mississippi, where an early morning bell summons the slaves to labor.

l: Arkansas, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Arkansas contains the large estate that Steve Brindle says S. S. Simon left to Cæsar Simon.

l: Paducah, Kentucky, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Paducah, Kentucky, is where Cæsar Simon, using the name Cole Conway, joins Steve Sharp in gambling. After they lose their last money, the two sleep in an old straw shed outside the village.

l: the decade from 1840 to 1850, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The decade from 1840 to 1850 is described as one of the most important periods in the settlement and progress of the Western States. During it, the iron horse and magnetic telegraph begin successful operation across the region.

l: the settlement and progress of the Western States, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The settlement and progress of the Western States accelerate during the decade from 1840 to 1850. New transportation and communication technologies contribute to this transformation.

l: cotton cultivation, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Cotton cultivation in the Southern States expands to gigantic proportions during the first half of the nineteenth century. Young Simon becomes a cotton planter through his inheritance.

l: slavery, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Slavery is central to the plantation economy described in the unit. Young Simon inherits more than six hundred slaves, and S. S. Simon's demand for labor leads him to have them summoned before daylight.

l: the iron horse, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The iron horse is identified as one of the great motive powers of modern civilization. It is successfully put into operation across the Western States during the decade from 1840 to 1850.

l: the magnetic telegraph, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The magnetic telegraph is identified with the iron horse as a major force in modern civilization. It is successfully put into operation across the Western States during the decade from 1840 to 1850.

l: the Simon estate, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Young Simon's estate includes four plantations of one thousand acres each and more than six hundred slaves inherited from S. S. Simon. Steve Brindle later describes S. S. Simon's estate in Arkansas as one of the largest.

l: the Simon plantations, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: S. S. Simon's plantations consist of four plantations of one thousand acres each. Their labor is organized through an early morning bell that calls the slaves to work before daylight.

l: the slaves on S. S. Simon's plantations, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The slaves on S. S. Simon's plantations number more than six hundred. They are required to be ready to resume work as soon as they can see each morning.

l: the dream of the steam carriage, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: In his dream, Cæsar Simon sees a steam carriage, finds gold and a rule containing directions, and travels south with Steve Brindle. The dream includes a speed gauge, a boiler, and a pump-like handle that seems to draw water from the dry road; Brindle interprets it as a sign of Cæsar's inheritance.

l: the steam carriage, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: The steam carriage is imagined as a light, four-wheeled vehicle carrying six passengers. It has a pilot on top, an engineer and fireman at the rear, a polished brass boiler, and a chemical heat source made from phosphorus and tinder.

l: death, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SIXTH.
s: Death is presented as a gradual succession in which old people pass away and new people take their places. S. S. Simon dies from swamp fever, and Young Simon follows him after a short life marked by poor health.

l: Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Roxie Daymon, the penniless daughter of Roxie Fairfield, joins a pleasure party traveling from Chicago to New Orleans and meets young Simon, a wealthy but terminally ill cotton planter. After learning that Roxie may be connected to heirs of a twenty-thousand-dollar claim against Simon’s estate, Simon becomes convinced of a mystery involving her family and becomes engaged to her. When Simon returns to Chicago in April 1861, his health fails, and he dictates a will leaving his entire estate, worth more than a million dollars, to Roxie. After Simon’s death, cousin Cæsar hires Gov. Morock to challenge the will and pays him one thousand dollars in advance.

l: Roxie Daymon (daughter), Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Roxie Daymon is left penniless after every case concerning her property goes against her. She travels with a pleasure party to New Orleans, becomes engaged to young Simon, and is named sole beneficiary of his estate after his death.

l: Governor Morock, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Gov. Morock tells Roxie that she is destitute and offers, for fifty dollars, to arrange a legal loophole or “shadow” to marry her off. Later, he writes young Simon’s will for ten dollars and agrees to challenge it for cousin Cæsar, taking one thousand dollars in advance and planning to charge additional sums.

l: Young Simon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Young Simon is in the last stage of consumption and travels toward New Orleans and the West Indies in search of relief. He learns of the mystery surrounding Roxie Daymon’s family, becomes engaged to her, returns to Chicago, dictates a will in her favor, and dies shortly afterward.

l: Cæsar Simon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Cousin Cæsar knows much of the circumstances surrounding Roxie and Simon but initially keeps them to himself. He tells Simon the story, accompanies him, hires Gov. Morock to break the will after Simon’s death, pays one thousand dollars in advance, and then travels to Kentucky to seek help from Cliff Carlo.

l: the pleasure party, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: The pleasure party consists of young people from Chicago, including four or five young ladies and Roxie Daymon. Its members agree to pay Roxie’s expenses and travel by steamer to New Orleans before returning to Chicago.

l: Chicago, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Chicago is where Roxie lives among the city’s moneyed aristocracy, where the pleasure party is formed, and where Simon returns before his death. It is also the place where Roxie and Simon are expected to marry.

l: New Orleans, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: New Orleans is the destination of the pleasure trip taken by Roxie Daymon and the young people from Chicago. Young Simon and cousin Cæsar also travel there before continuing toward the West Indies.

l: the Simon estate, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Young Simon’s estate is reported to be worth more than a million dollars. After his death, the entire estate is left to Roxie Daymon, prompting cousin Cæsar to seek legal action against the inheritance.

l: the Simon will, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Gov. Morock writes a will dictated by young Simon that bequeaths all of Simon’s possessions, without reserve, to Roxie Daymon. After Simon’s death, cousin Cæsar seeks to break the will by alleging that Simon lacked capacity.

l: the inheritance dispute, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: The inheritance dispute begins when cousin Cæsar objects to Roxie Daymon receiving young Simon’s entire estate. Gov. Morock advises Cæsar to challenge the will and accepts one thousand dollars in advance to undertake the case.

l: the pleasure trip to New Orleans, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: The trip is arranged in October by a group of young people living in Chicago. The party travels on the steamer Roman Eagle, where Roxie meets young Simon and the mystery concerning her family is raised.

l: Roxie Daymon and Young Simon’s engagement, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Roxie Daymon and young Simon become engaged after the trip and are expected to marry the following spring in Chicago. Simon continues to think of Roxie despite seeing many beautiful women during his travels.

l: Roxie Daymon and Young Simon’s proposed marriage, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: The proposed marriage is set for the spring of 1861 in Chicago. It is postponed when Simon returns seriously ill and can no longer stand alone.

l: Young Simon’s death, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Young Simon dies in Chicago after cousin Cæsar keeps vigil beside him through the night. His remains are prepared for transport to Arkansas, where he is to be buried beside his father.

l: poverty and destitution, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Roxie Daymon is told that she has lost everything and is hopelessly destitute and penniless. She replies that her mother was once a poor, penniless girl and that she can endure poverty as well.

l: Roxie Daymon’s family history, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Roxie Daymon, whose death has been recorded, left an only daughter, now grown to
s: Roxie says that her mother was Roxie Fairfield, an orphan girl raised in Kentucky. Aunt Patsy Perkins told her that her mother had two sisters, Rose and Suza, whom she called poor trash; cousin Cæsar later learns that Roxie is connected to heirs of a twenty-thousand-dollar claim with twenty years of interest against Simon’s estate.

l: Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The unit follows Cousin Cæsar Simon through the early years of the War Between the States, especially his service in General Sterling Price’s army in Missouri and Arkansas. Cæsar is wounded at the battle of Wilson’s Creek, rescued by Steve Brindle and a Cherokee Indian, and later becomes troubled by the recurring number 77 and by his neglect of Steve. The unit also describes Roxie Daymon and Governor Morock’s efforts to profit from the Simon estate and challenge the Simon will. Cliff Carlo joins the Southern armies, while the war devastates Missouri, Arkansas, and the Simon plantations.

l: Cæsar Simon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Cousin Cæsar Simon leaves Kentucky for Missouri to consult members of the Carlo family and joins General Sterling Price’s army. He fights at Wilson’s Creek, is severely wounded in the leg, and is rescued by Steve Brindle and a Cherokee Indian. He later worries over the recurring number 77, neglects to acknowledge Steve when he is prosperous, and considers whether Steve’s reported desertion is a message intended for him.

l: Cliff Carlo, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Cliff Carlo counsels with Cousin Cæsar about the expenses of contesting the Simon estate, but remains non-committal because Roxie Daymon is a near relative. He later writes to Governor Morock for information about the estate and joins the Southern armies, passing through the war without sickness or wounds.

l: Roxie Daymon, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Roxie Daymon spends the summer and fall in Chicago with a reputation for wealth, although she receives no dividends from the Simon estate. She consults Governor Morock about challenging the Simon will and authorizes him to try to obtain cotton from the Simon plantations.

l: Steve Brindle, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Steve Brindle serves as a private in General Pearce’s army and saves Cousin Cæsar’s life at Wilson’s Creek with the help of a Cherokee Indian. He has previously shared his money and family history with Cæsar, but Cæsar later refuses to acknowledge him when surrounded by wealth and power. After the battle at Elkhorn, Steve is reported to have been wounded, and a card stating that Cæsar Simon had deserted is associated with him.

l: Governor Morock, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Governor Morock tells Roxie Daymon that money can help break the Simon will and offers to arrange testimony. He proposes to obtain cotton from the Simon plantations through a federal officer, but his agents secure no crumbs despite his use of nearly all of the thousand dollars obtained from Cousin Cæsar.

l: General Sterling Price, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: General Sterling Price commands an improvised Southern army in Missouri during the first year of the war. His army marches extensively, fights the Federals wherever it finds them, captures supplies and weapons, and later moves north to Lexington before retreating south.

l: the late civil war between the States of the American Union, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The late civil war between the States of the American Union is described as the result of two civilizations existing under one government. The unit emphasizes its effects on the characters, including military service, divided loyalties, deaths, wounds, economic opportunism, and the destruction of property.

l: War Between the States, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The War Between the States begins after the firing on Fort Sumter and the opposing calls to arms in the North and South. It draws Cousin Cæsar, Cliff Carlo, and many others into military service and destroys the Simon plantations.

l: Kentucky, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Kentucky initially claims to be the holy ground of peace and remains in the Union, a position Cousin Cæsar considers inadequate. In the second year of the war, Kentucky is invaded on both sides, and Cliff Carlo joins the Southern armies.

l: Missouri, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Missouri is invaded by federal troops and becomes the principal theater of General Sterling Price’s first-year campaign. Price’s poorly equipped army marches more than eight hundred miles across Missouri and repeatedly engages Federal forces.

l: Springfield, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Springfield is the usual name given to the battle of Oak Hill, where Federal troops under General Lyon fought Confederate forces under Generals McCulloch, Price, and Pearce. Cousin Cæsar is wounded there after General Lyon is killed and the Federals retreat.

l: Arkansas, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Arkansas is the state where the legal contest over the Simon estate takes place. The unit also states that Steve Brindle served in Price’s army from Arkansas and that the Simon plantations were located there.

l: Chicago, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Chicago is described as a loyal city where Roxie Daymon lives during the first year of the war. Roxie meets Governor Morock at his office on Strait street to discuss the Simon estate, the Simon will, and the possible recovery of cotton.

l: the Simon estate, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The Simon estate is the subject of a legal contest involving Cousin Cæsar, Cliff Carlo, Roxie Daymon, and Governor Morock. Governor Morock tells Cliff Carlo that it is worth more than a million and a quarter, while the Simon plantations and residence are later devastated by fire.

l: the Simon will, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The Simon will is threatened with a legal challenge by Cousin Cæsar and Roxie Daymon. Governor Morock claims that money could break it and proposes arranging testimony concerning Simon’s mental faculties.

l: the federal government, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The federal government calls for troops after Fort Sumter and sends federal forces into Missouri. During the first year of the war, it announces that it will not interfere with the slaves of loyal men.

l: the Confederate States of America, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The Confederate States of America provide no promised pay or assistance to General Price’s initial Missouri army, which nevertheless takes the field using weapons and supplies gathered from citizens and captured from Federal forces.

l: the Union, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The Union loses the border slave States when they withdraw and join the South, except for Kentucky, which remains inactive in the hope of peace. The war then brings Federal military operations into Missouri and other contested regions.

l: the federal army, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The federal army invades Missouri and is placed under the command of General Lyon. It fights Price’s forces at Springfield and Wilson’s Creek, retreats after Lyon’s death, and later occupies the fortified position at Lexington before its capture.

l: Price’s army, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: Price’s army is an unpaid and poorly equipped volunteer force made up of people from many occupations and ages. It survives on irregular provisions, captures weapons and equipment from the Federals, fights across Missouri, and later crosses the Mississippi River.

l: the battle of Wilson’s Creek, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The battle of Wilson’s Creek, also called the battle of Oak Hill or Springfield, takes place on August 10, 1861. General Lyon is killed while leading a charge, the Federals retreat, and Cousin Cæsar receives a painful gunshot wound in the right leg.

l: the first year of the war in Missouri, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The first year of the war in Missouri is portrayed as an unusually harsh campaign in which Price’s army marches more than eight hundred miles, often lacks food and equipment, and fights frequent engagements. Despite these hardships, the army remains cheerful and is said never to lose a battle on Missouri soil during that year.

l: the 77 superstition, Pen Pictures of Eventful Scenes and Struggles of Life, SCENE SEVENTH--WAR BETWEEN THE STATES.
s: The 77 superstition troubles Cousin Cæsar after he is assigned the number 77 and later receives a card bearing the same number. He interprets Steve Brindle’s message that Cæsar Simon had deserted as possibly meaning that Steve had 'fallen off' and wanted Cæsar to follow him.

s: The federals fortified Helena with three forts and a gunboat and were attacked by General Holmes's approximately 4,900 men on July 4, 1863. General Price carried the center position, but Marmaduke and Fagan failed to carry the other forts, and Price's men later retreated with heavy losses. Cæsar Simon fell at Helena, ending the Simon family in the male line. Nearly two years later the Southern soldiers surrendered, the war ended, the Simon land was sold to pay judgments, and the surviving named figures went on to different postwar lives.

s: The battle took place at Helena on the holiday of American Independence. General Price carried one position, but the other positions held, and the retreat was made under deadly enemy fire.

s: Cæsar Simon observed the battle while crouched beneath an old stump and recognized Steve Brindle among the federal soldiers. He fell at Helena, and his death ended the Simon family in the male line.

s: The war continued for nearly two more years after the battle at Helena. It ended when the weary and war-worn Southern soldiers, sadly deficient in numbers, laid down their arms.

s: The Simon family lost its last male-line link when Cæsar Simon fell. After the war, the Simon plantations and the last foot of Simon land were lost through sales.

s: The Simon plantations were affected by President Lincoln's proclamation of freedom, which removed the monetary value of the slaves held there.

s: The last foot of the Simon land was sold at sheriff's sale to pay judgments described as just and unjust.

s: Governor Morock retired from the profession, or the profession retired from him. He lived on the cheap sale of a bad reputation, performing dirty work at a low price for those who employed him.

s: Roxie Daymon married a young mechanic and was happy in a cottage home. She tried to blot out the memory of the past by reading "The Workman's Saturday Night."
